headline: Illinois hemp sellers sue to stop Hemp Act before 12 November start
dek: A trade group for 250 hemp firms asked a Chicago federal court to freeze Illinois' 0.4 mg THC cap, arguing it shuts out interstate sellers a month early.
key_points: The Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association and five hemp businesses filed suit in federal court in Chicago on 5 November, seeking an emergency order against the Illinois Hemp Act.
From 12 November, any consumable or topical product with more than 0.4 mg of total THC per container becomes cannabis in Illinois and can only be sold through licensed dispensaries.
The plaintiffs argue the law breaks the Commerce Clause because the same products stay federally lawful until the national ban starts on 11 December.
No ruling on the restraining order had been reported as of 8 November, leaving operators days to plan for either outcome.
body: Illinois' hemp industry has gone to federal court to stop the state's new Hemp Act before it takes effect on Thursday, 12 November. The Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association, a trade group that says it represents 250 companies employing more than 5,000 people, filed a complaint and an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order in the US District Court for the Northern District of Illinois on 5 November. Five hemp businesses joined the filing.

The case, Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association v. Raoul (No. 1:26-cv-13799), names Attorney General Kwame Raoul and the heads of five state agencies: Agriculture, Financial and Professional Regulation, State Police, Revenue and Public Health. It asks a judge to block the parts of the law that turn most of the intoxicating hemp products sold today into "cannabis" that only licensed dispensaries may sell. Unless the court acts within days, THC drinks, gummies and similar goods above the new limit leave non-dispensary shelves in Illinois a full month before the matching federal ban begins on 11 December.
## What the Hemp Act changes

Under Public Act 104-0463, any consumable or topical product holding more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container stops counting as hemp in Illinois, according to a bulletin the Illinois Department of Revenue issued on 14 October. Those products become cannabis under the state's Cannabis Regulation and Tax Act and may only be grown and sold by businesses licensed under it. Products that fit the new category of a "final consumer hemp cannabinoid product" can still be sold under the Hemp Act itself.

The per-container cap is what reshapes the market. Most THC drinks and gummies carry several milligrams of THC per serving, not fractions of one, so a 0.4 mg ceiling removes nearly every intoxicating product now sold in breweries, convenience stores and smoke shops. The Revenue bulletin tells businesses to check their stock now so they are not left holding or selling unlicensed cannabis after the start date.
The Act also measures hemp by total THC above 0.3% on a dry-weight basis rather than delta-9 THC alone, which moves high-THCA flower into the cannabis column as well.
## The constitutional argument

The plaintiffs' central claim is that the law violates the Commerce Clause of the US Constitution. Their emergency motion asks the court to stop the state from applying the new hemp definition and the 0.4 mg cap, from blocking out-of-state companies that sell federally legal hemp products into Illinois, from preventing Illinois buyers from sourcing hemp from other states, and from requiring hemp businesses to hold cannabis licences.

The calendar is the heart of the case. Congress rewrote the federal definition of hemp in its November 2025 funding law, and a later stopgap pushed the start of that change to 11 December 2026. For 29 days, from 12 November to 11 December, the products at issue remain lawful under federal law across most of the country but illegal under Illinois' new definitions. The industry argues the state is using that window to close its market to interstate trade in goods Congress still permits.

The complaint also says the Act suffers from other constitutional defects, according to Block Club Chicago, which first reported the filing. As of the latest public record, no order granting or denying the restraining order had been reported, and the filed papers did not yet show an assigned judge.
## What is at stake

The trade group puts last year's Illinois hemp sales at more than $500 million, with about $30 million going to the state in revenue, Block Club reported. Those are industry figures and have not been independently verified.

THC beverages have become an important product line for some Chicago craft brewers facing a shrinking beer market, the outlet reported, naming Revolution, Hopewell and Marz. A Hopewell co-founder told Block Club the law would eliminate the THC drink category. Some brands are already clearing stock and halting production, and one beverage company organised a "last call" toast event in Chicago ahead of the deadline.

State leaders say tighter rules are needed to protect consumers, particularly children, from unregulated products with misleading labels and packaging, CBS Chicago reported on 8 November. Gov. JB Pritzker, Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton and Sen. Tammy Duckworth went further last week, urging Congress to let the federal hemp THC ban start without more delay, as we reported on 7 November.
> Illinois wants to close its hemp market a month before Washington does. A judge now has days, not weeks, to decide whether that month is a state's right or a barrier to interstate trade.
## Why licensed operators are watching

For Illinois' licensed dispensaries, the Act would route demand that now goes to hemp retailers into the regulated channel, where products are tested and taxed. Our 6 November report set out how the state cliff lands ahead of the federal one, and why the gap matters for both sides.

Illinois is not alone on the date. Missouri's own 0.4 mg per container limit also begins on 12 November, after a judge dismissed a hemp industry challenge there and Attorney General Catherine Hanaway sued four retailers accused of selling marijuana labelled as hemp. If both states' laws stand, two large Midwestern markets switch over on the same day.

Even a win for the Illinois plaintiffs would buy limited time. Unless Congress acts, the federal redefinition still arrives on 11 December. Bills to undo it, such as Rep. Nancy Mace's American Hemp Protection Act, have sat in a House Agriculture subcommittee since January, according to Congress.gov. Block Club noted pending legislation that would push the federal deadline to 2028; it has not passed.
## What to watch

The first marker is a ruling on the restraining order before 12 November. If the court declines, enforcement starts on schedule and the case moves to the slower preliminary injunction track. If it grants relief, an appeal to the Seventh Circuit is likely. Either way, 11 December is the next hard date, when the federal total-THC definition and its 0.4 mg per container cap take effect nationwide. Retailers holding hemp THC inventory in Illinois should expect the state's Revenue and Public Health agencies to publish enforcement guidance if the law takes effect.
